paper_title: AV-FABLE: Audio-Visual Manipulation Forensics in Long-Form Videos

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Localized AI manipulations in long-form videos often affect brief events within otherwise authentic content, making video-level classification insufficient for forensic analysis. Existing audio-visual deepfake benchmarks largely focus on short talking-head clips, while long-form temporal forensics remains predominantly visual. We introduce AV-FABLE, a dual-timeline benchmark for sparse manipulations in open-scene long-form audio-visual videos. AV-FABLE contains 16,650 pristine--manipulated twin pairs (998 hours) created with 27 editing configurations, with separate audio and visual timelines that enable modality-specific temporal localization and expose errors hidden by joint-timeline evaluation. On AV-FABLE, zero-shot prompting of audio-visual large language models (AV-LLMs) yields near-chance detection and poor temporal localization. In contrast, supervised readouts of their frozen perception features recover strong forensic signals, suggesting manipulation evidence is encoded in these representations but not effectively exposed through language outputs. Motivated by this observation, we propose NFSR(Native Forensics via Separated Readouts), which reads frozen AV-LLM features with separate audio and visual temporal decoders. NFSR achieves the best audio-visual localization performance in-domain and across all three out-of-distribution settings, including transfer to held-out videos from an external long-video forensic benchmark. AV-FABLE, code, and model weights will be publicly released.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: A few manipulated seconds can change the meaning of an otherwise authentic video. Replacing an utterance can alter what speaker appears to have said; inserting sound can suggest an event that never occurred; modifying brief action can change the interpretation of an entire sequence. Such edits may affect the audio, the visual stream, or both, often with different temporal boundaries. video-level authenticity label therefore reveals little about where manipulation occurs or which modality is affected. Fine-grained forensic analysis requires identifying when manipulation occurred and which modality was affected. Existing benchmarks capture parts of this problem, but not this setting as whole. LAV-DF and the AV-Deepfake1M series advance audio-visual deepfake detection and temporal localization in predominantly speaker-centered videos (Cai et al., 2022; 2024; 2025). TASLE and ActivityForensics extend visual forensics to localized manipulations in broader, untrimmed videos (Feng et al., 2026; Bao et al., 2026), while AVID studies audio-visual inconsistency understanding and temporal grounding in long-form videos (Chen et al., 2026b). What remains missing is benchmark that localizes manipulations independently on the audio and visual timelines of open-scene long-form video. This distinction is important because audio and visual edits may overlap, occur asynchronously, or affect only one modality. We target this setting: sparse manipulations of speech, environmental sounds, actions, objects, and attributes embedded within largely authentic long-form content. The distinction between modalities is central to this setting. Audio and visual manipulations may overlap in time, occur asynchronously, or affect only one modality. joint timeline can therefore reward prediction for finding the right moment even when it identifies the wrong stream. Cross1 Figure 1: Overview of SEE-Forge, the event-driven pipeline for constructing AV-FABLE. Given an event in pristine video, SEE-Forge plans audio and/or visual manipulations, executes them with editors, and reinserts them into context to create pristinemanipulated twin pairs. The executed interval provides temporal ground truth, while human-reviewed annotations record forensic cues within and around the manipulated event. modal consistency is also insufficient: two streams can remain plausible even when one has been altered. Evaluation should therefore preserve both temporal boundaries and modality identity. We introduce AV-FABLE (Forensic Audio-visual Benchmark for Long-form Events), dual-timeline benchmark for sparse manipulations in open-scene long-form audio-visual videos. AV-FABLE comprises 16,650 pristinemanipulated twin pairs spanning 998 hours and 27 editing configurations; videos are minute-scale (median 88 s), and manipulations cover median of 9.45% of each manipulated video. Our construction pipeline, SEE-Forge, selects natural events in the source footage, plans local audio or visual edit for each, routes the edit to suitable generator, and reinserts the result into the original video (Figure 1). Each manipulated video has pristine twin from the same source under matched export process, reducing content and processing confounds. Separate audio and visual timelines record the interval and modality of every executed edit, and human-verified evidence records describe how each edit can be observed. The benchmark centers on temporal localization, together with detection, modality attribution, and explanation, and evaluates transfer to held-out sources, generators, and editing routes with thresholds fixed on source-domain data. Native-track evaluation exposes failures that joint-timeline evaluation hides: the visual predictions of our model alone reach 64.04 Joint-mAP, above every visual-only baseline, while missing every audio event. When prompted zero-shot on AV-FABLE, the audio-visual large language models (AV-LLMs) Qwen2.5-Omni and Qwen3-Omni (Xu et al., 2025a;b) reach only 5152 detection AUROC and at most 0.30 mAP on either track. Yet linear probes on their frozen perception features separate manipulated from authentic segments with 90.8 (audio) and 80.8 (visual) AUROC. This striking gap suggests that AV-LLMs encode useful forensic evidence in their perceptual representations, but fail to reliably expose it through zero-shot language outputs. This observation motivates learning temporal readouts directly from these frozen features. Building on this finding, we propose NFSR (Native Forensics via Separated Readouts), which directly reads frozen audio and visual representations for modality-specific temporal localization. NFSR combines intermediate-layer and interface features, conditions local evidence on the host video, and uses separate temporal decoders to localize audio and visual manipulations. Their predictions further support video-level detection and modality attribution. In-domain, NFSR achieves 91.30 AV-mAP and 96.04 detection AUROC, compared with 84.76 AV-mAP for UMMAFormer using the same frozen features. NFSR further achieves the highest AV-mAP across all three OOD settings, including transfer to source-disjoint subset of the external TASLE benchmark. Our contributions are summarized as follows: AV-FABLE and the dual-timeline task: large-scale benchmark for sparse audio-visual temporal localization in long-form videos, with pristinemanipulated twin pairs, separate 2 audio and visual annotations, and three OOD settings. Its native-track evaluation exposes failures hidden by joint-timeline evaluation. finding on AV-LLMs: zero-shot prompting remains near chance on AV-FABLE, while supervised readouts of frozen perception features recover strong forensic signals, revealing gap between internal representations and language outputs. NFSR: readout of frozen AV-LLM encoders that combines intermediate-layer and interface features, host conditioning, and separate audio and visual decoders. NFSR achieves the highest AV-mAP in-domain and across all three OOD settings.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Benchmarks for manipulation detection and temporal localization. Facial-forgery benchmarks primarily assess imageor video-level authenticity (Rossler et al., 2019; Li et al., 2020; Dolhansky et al., 2020), with FakeAVCeleb adding manipulated speech to talking-head video (Khalid et al., 2021). ForgeryNet and PartialSpoof provide interval-level supervision for visual and audio manipulations, respectively (He et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2023a). LAV-DF and the AV-Deepfake1M series extend temporal localization to content-driven audio-visual edits, predominantly in speaker-centered clips (Cai et al., 2022; 2023; 2024; 2025). Beyond this setting, AVFakeBench broadens scene coverage (Xia et al., 2026), while Omni-Fake brings several media types into common forensic benchmark (Li et al., 2026b). Longer authentic context is central to TASLE and ActivityForensics, which embed sparse visual manipulations within untrimmed or activity-rich videos (Feng et al., 2026; Bao et al., 2026). AVID studies long-form audio-visual inconsistency grounding (Chen et al., 2026b), but cross-modal compatibility and the authenticity of each stream remain distinct targets. AVFABLE combines open-scene long-form videos with separate temporal annotations and native-track evaluation, requiring both manipulation boundaries and the affected modality to be identified. Temporal localization and forensic representations. Beyond classification (Chollet, 2017; Jung et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2026a), temporal forensics studies boundary prediction in audio (Wu et al., 2024; Zhong et al., 2024) and audio-visual content (Cai et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2025b; Shen et al., 2026). Audio-visual localizers exploit cross-modal cues (Koutlis & Papadopoulos, 2026; Anshul et al., 2025), adaptive features in UMMAFormer (Zhang et al., 2023b), or query-based and contextual modeling (Zhu et al., 2025; Yin et al., 2026). Action detection supplies interval predictors (Zhang et al., 2022), while TASLEs MSLoc uses language-assisted proposal refinement (Feng et al., 2026). Modality-decoupled detectors retain stream-specific evidence (Peng et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026a). AV-LLMs provide language-based predictions (Xu et al., 2025a;b; Tang et al., 2025), whereas supervised probes assess forensic information accessible from pretrained features (Alain & Bengio, 2016; Boldisor et al., 2026). NFSR conditions frozen perception features on the input host video and learns separate audio and visual temporal readouts. Appendix expands these comparisons and reviews generation and editing techniques.

Predictions on pristine videos count as false positives under both protocols, as do predictions on an unmodified track under native-track evaluation. 3.2 EVENT-DRIVEN CONSTRUCTION AND ANNOTATION From natural events to executable edits. SEE-Forge (Figure 1) edits events that already occur in the host video, i.e., the source video that receives the edit, rather than arbitrary time windows. ActivityNet (Heilbron et al., 2015) and EPIC-KITCHENS-100 (Damen et al., 2022) provide thirdperson activities and egocentric interactions; HDTF (Zhang et al., 2021) supplies held-out talking-head videos. For each host video, we build an event catalog from captions, speech transcripts, acoustic onsets, motion, and object interactions. Gemini 3.7 Flash (Google DeepMind, 2026) then acts as the planner: it selects one cataloged event and specifies the target track, interval, semantic change, and content to preserve. second model verifies that the target is observable and that compatible generator can execute the instruction. Editing and pristine twins. Each of the 27 editing configurations pairs generator with an execution route: frame-conditioned generation, masked or unmasked video-to-video editing, joint audio-visual generation, audio generation, or speech replacement  (Table 6)  . SAM 2 masks constrain localized visual edits (Ravi et al., 2025). Generators receive the target interval with 25 of surrounding context, and their outputs are reinserted at the recorded coordinates with checks on motion continuity, visual anchors, and loudness at the seams. Each manipulated video has pristine twin from the same host video, and both twins pass through the same cropping, reinsertion, and export steps (resolution, frame rate, codec, and audio format). These controls address the content and processing shortcuts reported for earlier datasets (Smeu et al., 2025): metadata-only classifiers reach at most 54.6 AUROC  (Table 8)  . Traces that generators leave inside the edited interval, such as local resampling, generator texture, or synthesis residue, are beyond the reach of file-level probes and are discussed in Appendix A.5. The pristine twin also serves as content-matched reference for annotation and error analysis. Temporal labels and observable evidence. Temporal labels are execution-grounded: each event records the track, interval, operation, and target category of an executed edit, and ground truth refers to these annotations. Intervals mark where edits were applied rather than perceptual boundaries, so perceptible change may cover only part of an interval or begin and end slightly off its boundaries; reviewers check boundaries during retention but do not re-draw them. Operations cover replacement, insertion, regeneration, and removal; targets include speech, sounds, actions, objects, and scene content. For 20,529 events, Gemini 3.7 Flash drafts candidate evidence record from short clip around the event. Across manipulated videos, the union of audio and visual event intervals covers median of 9.45% of the video, while 91.5% have at most 30% manipulated time. Videos are minute-scale: the median lasts 88 and 80% last between 33 and 207 s. The median event lasts about 9 in the training and ID splits, so each manipulation occupies small part of its timeline. In 561 both-track videos, the audio and visual events do not overlap, so each track requires its own boundaries. We allocate 10,954/2,347/2,347/1,002 twin pairs to training, validation, in-domain (ID) testing, and OOD testing; all derivatives of host video remain in the same split. Of the 27 editing configurations, 23 appear in training and four are held out. We evaluate three OOD settings (Section 5.2): source transfer to HDTF and source-disjoint TASLE subset, held-out generators on seen routes, and heldout TI2V, text-and-image-conditioned video generation route withheld together with its generator. Evaluation covers localization, detection, attribution, and explanation, with decision thresholds fixed on source-validation data (Section 5). Explanation is the most challenging dimension: current baselines produce well-formed outputs but often misidentify the operation or target (Appendix H), leaving substantial room for future work. sections.title: 5 EXPERIMENTS
sections.content: We evaluate whether frozen perception features support sparse audio-visual temporal localization, how the resulting readouts transfer to the three OOD settings, and how feature depth, host conditioning, and modality separation affect these results. Evaluation protocol. We use AV-FABLEs source-disjoint splits. Localization uses confidenceranked mAP@[0.30:0.05:0.70] and Event-IoU, the mean best overlap per event, with zero assigned to misses. AV-mAP, headline measure, averages A-mAP and V-mAP over tracks with events; method without output on track receives zero AP there. Joint-timeline metrics (Joint-mAP and Joint-IoU; Section 3.1) apply to outputs without track labels, but count correct co-timed prediction on the second track as duplicate, so we report them as an auxiliary view (Appendix C.3). Detection uses AUROC and realized false-alarm rate (FAR). Attribution reports macro-F1 over the four classes (clean, audio-only, visual-only, both-track) present in each evaluation sets ground truth (Eq. 5); held-out TI2V, for example, contains only clean and visual-only videos, so attribution is compared within rather than across settings. Thresholds are set on 256 pristine source-validation videos at nominal 5% FAR budget and held fixed on ID and OOD data (Appendix C). Baselines and implementation. We compare three prediction approaches: language-interface inference with Qwen2.5-Omni-7B, Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B, and video-SALMONN 2+ 7B (Xu et al., 2025a;b; Tang et al., 2025); single-modality detection with Xception (Chollet, 2017), AASIST (Jung et al., 2022), and DeMamba (Chen et al., 2026a); and temporal or audio-visual modeling with BATFD+ (Cai et al., 2023), ActionFormer (Zhang et al., 2022), UMMAFormer (Zhang et al., 2023b), AuViRe (Koutlis & Papadopoulos, 2026), ICS-Sync (Anshul et al., 2025), and DAV-Det (Peng et al., 2026). Qwen3-Omni timestamp SFT additionally tests supervised language-based localization. We include the released MSLoc proposal generator (Feng et al., 2026); its full pipeline and baseline adaptation details appear in Appendix and Appendix C, respectively. These groups differ in role and output form  (Table 2)  : AV-LLMs test whether prompted outputs expose manipulations, single-modality detectors are track-specific references, and localizers with separate audio and visual interval outputs are the direct comparison. For fixed-window, single-track, unified, and text outputs, localization scores also reflect the fit of the output form to the task; AV-FABLE-trained AASIST, for example, reaches 75.95 AUROC but 0.06 A-mAP after window-to-interval conversion. Zero-shot AV-LLM predictions yield near-chance detection and at most 0.30 mAP on either track  (Table 2)  , partly because of their text-timestamp output. Timestamp SFT keeps this output form and raises A-mAP to 57.30 but V-mAP only to 18.30. On the same frozen features, linear probes outperform unsupervised feature-deviation and temporal-jump scores on both tracks  (Table 15)  , and NFSR reaches 92.24 A-mAP and 90.36 V-mAP. The forensic evidence is therefore accessible to supervised readouts even when prompted outputs do not reveal it. NFSR improves localization on shared frozen features. With the same Qwen3 features and training budget, NFSR raises AV-mAP over UMMAFormer from 84.76 to 91.30, the highest in Table 2, with the largest gain on the visual track (+10.74 V-mAP). It also improves detection AUROC by 6.86 points and Event-IoU on both tracks, so the gain covers event coverage as well as ranking. NFSR also achieves the highest attribution F1. The AV-FABLE-trained ActionFormer is competitive on the visual track (89.22 V-mAP and higher V-IoU than NFSR); its lower AV-mAP reflects its visual-only output rather than weaker visual localization. sections.title: 6 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We introduce AV-FABLE, dual-timeline benchmark for localizing sparse audio and visual manipulations in open-scene long-form videos. By preserving both temporal boundaries and modality identity, AV-FABLE exposes failures that joint-timeline evaluation can miss. Our experiments reveal clear gap in current AV-LLMs: zero-shot prompting remains near chance, while supervised readouts of frozen perceptual representations recover strong forensic signals. Building on this observation, NFSR achieves the highest AV-mAP in-domain and across all three OOD settings, showing the effectiveness of modality-separated temporal readouts for long-form audio-visual forensics. Limitation and future direction. AV-FABLE also opens several directions for future research. Extending the benchmark to broader real-world editing processes, refining perceptual boundary annotations, improving robustness to media corruption, and developing more faithful evidence-grounded explanations are promising next steps. We will publicly release the dataset, code, and model weights to support further work in long-form audio-visual forensics.

sections.title: AI USE STATEMENT
sections.content: Generative AI models were used in the SEE-Forge pipeline to construct AV-FABLE, including event-level edit planning, localization of source events, edit-feasibility checks, audio and visual media generation and editing, and drafting candidate evidence annotations (Section 3.2 and Appendix A). Temporal manipulation labels were derived from the executed edits. Two reviewers independently assessed edit validity and evidence support using the edited media, pristine counterparts, and edit instructions, with disagreements adjudicated by third reviewer. Events without supported evidence records were retained for detection and localization but not explanation. AI tools also provided language assistance during manuscript preparation. The authors take responsibility for the final manuscript, results, and accompanying artifacts.

sections.title: ETHICS STATEMENT
sections.content: This work aims to advance research on audio-visual manipulation detection, localization, and forensic analysis in long-form videos. AV-FABLE builds on existing research datasets and introduces controlled manipulations using generative models. We follow the access and usage terms of the corresponding source datasets and do not redistribute source media, or excerpts thereof, when such redistribution is restricted by third-party licenses. The public release will instead focus on event-level annotations, source identifiers and timestamps, provenance metadata, independently releasable generated assets, and reconstruction utilities. Beyond long-form localization, these generated segments, produced by recent video, audio, and joint audio-visual generators across 27 editing configurations, can also serve as standalone resource: labeled with generator, route, and operation and paired through source timestamps with their pristine counterparts, they support real-versus-generated classification, and those with human-verified evidence records additionally support evidence-grounded explanation. Given the dual-use nature of deepfake research, we do not provide end-to-end pipelines intended for impersonation, fraud, or other malicious uses, and we avoid intentionally constructing defamatory or deceptive content targeting real individuals. Human review is used solely for data and annotation quality control. Additional details on data licensing, human review, and release policies are provided in the Appendix. REPRODUCIBILITY STATEMENT The reproducibility materials comprise the complete AV-FABLE dataset manifest; the split, OODsetting, and threshold-calibration lists; an independent evaluator with unit tests; and the model code with the training configuration. AV-FABLE, the code, and model weights will be publicly released in accordance with the source-data terms described in the Ethics statement. Additional implementation and dataset construction details are provided in the Appendix.

AV-FABLE: CONSTRUCTION AND DATA QUALITY A.1 SOURCES, COMPOSITION, AND LABELS ActivityNet-Raw supplies open-scene third-person videos, while EPIC-KITCHENS-100 supplies egocentric recordings (Heilbron et al., 2015; Damen et al., 2022). The EPIC construction pool contains 400 source recordings from 37 participants, totaling 67.3 hours; natural event clips are extracted before local manipulation and matched export. HDTF provides held-out talking-head hosts (Zhang et al., 2021). Source qualification checks decodability, both media tracks, synchronization, usable context, and observable candidate events. The release comprises 16,650 twin pairs and 22,153 track-specific events  (Table 5)  . The total of 998.1 hours sums both members of every pair; counting each pair once gives 499.1 hours. Video-level duration and coverage distributions count each pair once, whereas event statistics count the annotated intervals on each modality separately. The 16,650 manipulated videos contain 4,903 audio-only, 6,376 visual-only, and 5,371 both-track examples. Independent timelines allow events to overlap or occur asynchronously; jointly generated media can yield separate audio and visual event annotations. Event records include identity, track, interval, operation, target type, execution route, generator, and evidence status. Operations comprise replacement (14,914 events), insertion (5,555), regeneration (961), and removal (723). Targets cover sound events, actions, objects, attributes, ambience, speech, scene regions, text, and background. Table 5: Release statistics. The planner selects an existing event and specifies its modality, interval, single-action edit instruction, operation, target, preservation constraints, execution route, and expected evidence. Gemini 3.7 Flash plans (Google DeepMind, 2026), Qwen2.5-VL localizes (Bai et al., 2025), and Qwen3-Omni reviews plan validity and executability (Xu et al., 2025b). After execution, Gemini 3.7 Flash also drafts candidate evidence records from clip around each event. Checks establish that the target is observable, the requested change is compatible with its context, and the selected generator can execute the plan. Routing matches the edit to generator: masked V2V for local object/attribute changes, V2V for process changes, frame-conditioned generation for endpoint-constrained events, joint generation for audio-visual changes, and Foley/text-to-audio/TTS for audio edits. Generators receive the target interval and 25 seconds of context. Reinsertion preserves non-target content, checks visual anchors and motion continuity, and matches audio loudness with short cross-fades. Persistent entity changes require consistent editing across their visible intervals or replanning. Diversity memory controls repeated scene, target, operation, and generator combinations. Both twins then pass through common export profile, matching container, codec, resolution, frame rate, sample rate, channel count, and encoding policy. Pristine twins follow the same cropping, reinsertion, and export steps while retaining the original target content. DeeperForensics-1.0 and DF40 expand this setting through challenging perturbations and broader range of manipulation techniques (Jiang et al., 2020; Yan et al., 2024). Temporal supervision also appears in ForgeryNet, alongside imageand video-level face-forgery tasks (He et al., 2021). General generated-video resources such as GenVideo, GenVidBench, and AIGVDBench broaden the content and generators considered (Chen et al., 2026a; Ni et al., 2026; Ma et al., 2026a). Moving from wholly generated clips to sparse edits within video requires both broad content coverage and interval annotations. Partial speech manipulation and acoustic scenes. Speech anti-spoofing provides parallel route from recording-level decisions to within-recording localization. ASVspoof 2019 and ASVspoof 2021 establish protocols covering synthesized, converted, replayed, and deepfake speech (Wang et al., 2020; Yamagishi et al., 2021); WaveFake supplies synthetic speech from multiple generation methods (Frank & Schonherr, 2021). PartialSpoof, HAD, and ADD 2023 Track 2 focus more directly on partial manipulation or the localization of manipulated regions (Zhang et al., 2023a; Yi et al., 2021; 2023). Here, authentic and manipulated content can coexist within one recording, making global authenticity labels insufficient for boundary estimation. SceneFake broadens the manipulated content from speech to the surrounding acoustic scene (Yi et al., 2024). This distinction is relevant to environmental-sound edits, whose forensic evidence need not involve speaker or lip synchronization. Audio-visual benchmarks beyond talking heads. FakeAVCeleb combines facial and speech manipulations, establishing multimodal detection setting (Khalid et al., 2021). Within speaker-centered video, LAV-DF and AV-Deepfake1M provide content-driven edits with temporal annotations (Cai et al., 2022; 2024). AV-Deepfake1M++ extends this line with larger-scale evaluation under realistic perturbations (Cai et al., 2025). DDL-AV also retains fine-grained localization annotations across 23 audio, visual, and joint manipulations (Miao et al., 2025), while ArEnAV addresses ArabicEnglish code-switching and dialect variation (Kuckreja et al., 2026). More general audio-video content is represented by DDL-GAV, built on MVAD and described in DAV-Dets evaluation (Peng et al., 2026). The emphasis shifts toward forensic interpretation in X-AVFake and AVFakeBench, which include explanatory annotations or question-based evaluation beyond conventional talking-head detection (Chen et al., 2025a; Xia et al., 2026). Omni-Fake brings several media types into one benchmark, but its individual-modality localization tasks differ from its binary audio-video talking-head task (Li et al., 2026b). These benchmarks vary not only in content coverage but also in whether their labels supervise clip-level decisions or modality-specific intervals. Long-form context and modality-specific targets. Sparse edits within extended authentic context are central to TASLE and ActivityForensics, which study visual manipulation localization in untrimmed or activity-rich videos (Feng et al., 2026; Bao et al., 2026). AVID brings long-form context to audio-visual inconsistency understanding, including temporal grounding and reasoning about conflicting streams (Chen et al., 2026b). This shares the need to identify brief events, but an inconsistency target is not the same as establishing manipulation in each modality. replacement can remain semantically compatible with the other stream, and mismatch need not determine which stream was altered. AV-FABLE instead assigns executed edits to separate audio and visual timelines, including asynchronous events within the same host video. Native-track evaluation matches each prediction against its own modality, so temporally correct prediction on the wrong stream receives no credit. Reasoning resources and evaluation suites. Language-based forensic evaluation also depends on what evidence model can access. The datasets accompanying VidGuard-R1 and VideoVeritas, including the latters MintVid, support reasoning-oriented generated-video detection (Park et al., 2026; Tan et al., 2026a). EVID-Bench requires web retrieval and cross-video comparison to verify video misinformation, including cases not resolvable from the input video alone (Yu et al., 2026). It therefore differs from detecting local synthesis traces, even when AI-generated content contributes to the misinformation. DeepfakeBench standardizes detector implementation and evaluation (Yan et al., 2023), whereas FVBench assesses the deepfake-video detection capabilities of large multimodal models (Wang et al., 2026a). The extended comparison in Table 9 includes these evaluation resources alongside datasets without assuming that they share localization protocol. Spatial localization and explanation precedents. Image forensics provides relevant precedents for localized evidence, although its annotations refer to spatial regions rather than temporal intervals. DDL-I supplies image-forgery data and spatial annotations, complementing the DDL-AV branch (Miao et al., 2025). SID-Set and MMTD-Set-34k support SIDA and FakeShield, respectively, linking image detection and localization to explanatory supervision (Huang et al., 2025b; Xu et al., 2025c). HydraFake, introduced with Veritas, emphasizes generalization across forgery techniques and domains (Tan et al., 2026b); Impostor addresses realistic localized AI image editing (Li et al., 2026d). DFBench and the evaluation by Tariq et al. assess multimodal models on deepfake-image detection (Wang et al., 2025; Tariq et al., 2025). The 2-DFD annotation set further supports explainable deepfake detection (Chen et al., 2025c). They provide precedents for coupling localized evidence with explanation, while the temporal dimension requires different annotation target. Construction controls and generalization. The forensic task can be distorted when incidental processing traces predict the label. Circumventing Shortcuts identifies exploitable artifacts in audiovisual datasets (Smeu et al., 2025), while Fake or JPEG? and B-Free examine preprocessing and training-data biases in visual detection (Grommelt et al., 2024; Guillaro et al., 2025). These findings motivate matched processing of pristine and manipulated examples without implying that every synthesis trace should be removed. Likewise, held-out generator tests different shift from new source domain or editing route. When several factors change together, transfer measures the combined setting rather than an isolated causal effect of any one factor. B.2 GENERATION AND LOCALIZED EDITING Video generation models provide general synthesis capabilities (Yang et al., 2025; HaCohen et al., 2025; Wan et al., 2025), with further advances in controllable generation and world modeling (Ma et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026b; Zhang et al., 2026b; 2025b; 2026a). Related editing methods support controlled and streaming editing (Jiang et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026c), physics-grounded manipulation (Hu et al., 2026a), layer-decomposed editing (Liu et al., 2025b), as well as joint editing (Ma et al., 2026b). Diffusion-based methods also support controllable portrait animation, identity-consistent synthesis, and talking-head generation through visual or audio-visual conditioning (Xu et al., 2025d; Hu et al., 2026b; Hong et al., 2025). Speech can be replaced using synthesis systems such as F5-TTS and Qwen3-TTS (Chen et al., 2025d; Hu et al., 2026c). For non-speech audio, MMAudio and FoleyCrafter condition generation on visual content (Cheng et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026c), allowing an altered soundtrack to remain compatible with the visible scene. The same generator may produce fully synthetic clip or brief replacement inserted into an authentic host. The latter changes the forensic problem by retaining surrounding context and requiring event boundaries. In AV-FABLE, the executed edit coordinates define temporal ground truth, while the evidence records describe observable changes within and around those intervals. B.3 TEMPORAL LOCALIZATION AND FORENSIC REPRESENTATIONS From classification scores to event intervals. Single-modality detection provides useful references but does not always train an explicit boundary predictor. Xception supplies visual classification backbone (Chollet, 2017), AASIST targets speech anti-spoofing (Jung et al., 2022), and DeMamba models spatiotemporal evidence in generated videos (Chen et al., 2026a). Applying these detectors to successive windows produces local scores, but their conversion into intervals remains an additional modeling choice. correct video-level decision can therefore coexist with inaccurate boundaries or predictions assigned to the wrong modality. For partially spoofed audio, CFPRF combines frame-level predictions with proposal refinement (Wu et al., 2024); boundary-aware attention explicitly models genuinespoofed transitions (Zhong et al., 2024). These methods are closer to the interval-prediction objective than recording-level classification alone. Cross-modal evidence and temporal context. Audio-visual localization can use relationships between streams as forensic evidence, as in dissonance-based detection (Chugh et al., 2020). Crossmodal reconstruction and synchronization offer related cues in AuViRe and ICS-Sync (Koutlis & Papadopoulos, 2026; Anshul et al., 2025). Such cues must still be converted into temporal predictions: BA-TFD and BA-TFD+ emphasize boundary learning (Cai et al., 2022; 2023), and HBMNet combines frame-level and proposal-level boundary information (Chen et al., 2025b). UMMAFormer and RegQAV develop adaptive multimodal representations and query-based predictions, respectively (Zhang et al., 2023b; Zhu et al., 2025). UniCaCLF relates genuine and forged instants to global context through contrastive learning (Yin et al., 2026), while EVAS combines audio-visual interaction with boundary calibration (Shen et al., 2026). Together, these approaches connect evidence aggregation to boundary prediction, establishing context modeling as relevant precedent for long-form localization. Temporal decoding and host conditioning. Temporal action detection provides architectures that predict event intervals from feature sequences, including ActionFormer and DyFADet (Zhang et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2024). Their relevance is architectural: recognizing an action and deciding which part of it was manipulated remain different supervision targets. Action boundaries need not coincide with manipulation boundaries, even when the same temporal decoding architecture is used. Feature-wise linear modulation provides general mechanism for conditioning representation on contextual information (Perez et al., 2018). NFSR uses the input host videos feature statistics to modulate local evidence before modality-specific interval prediction. The pristine twin supports benchmark construction and annotation, but it is not required as reference at inference. Modality-specific decisions. Cross-modal evidence is informative but does not establish that both streams have been altered. DAV-Det models audio and visual forensic evidence independently (Peng et al., 2026), and Divide and Conquer combines modality-specific detectors and localizers through score fusion (Li et al., 2026a). Decoupled video-level detection and separate temporal predictions address different output requirements. The latter accommodates events with different boundaries in each stream, making modality identity part of the localization target. Frozen representations and language interfaces. Representation quality is different question from the behavior of language-based prediction interface. Linear probes assess information accessible through restricted supervised readouts (Alain & Bengio, 2016); self-supervised deepfake studies 25 examine the complementarity of audio and visual features (Boldisor et al., 2026). Qwen2.5-Omni, Qwen3-Omni, and video-SALMONN offer audio-visual language interfaces (Xu et al., 2025a;b; Tang et al., 2025), while AV-LMMDetect adapts an AV-LLM for authenticity classification (Cao et al., 2026). These settings differ in supervision, so weak zero-shot performance alone cannot establish that the underlying features lack useful forensic information. Section 5.1 compares temporal localizers on the same frozen features, separating the choice of encoder from the design of its readout. Language-assisted localization and explanation. language model may revise intervals or explain them, and these roles should be distinguished. TASLEs MSLoc uses language-assisted proposal refinement as part of visual localization (Feng et al., 2026). VidForensics-M1 incorporates verifiable temporal grounding into reinforcement learning through evidence-guided reward redistribution (Liu et al., 2026). PATE-Forensics separates forensic perception from explanation generation (Li et al., 2026c); FakeHunter retrieves contextual evidence and invokes tools to support multimodal reasoning (Chen et al., 2025a). Image-level systems likewise connect detected spatial regions to natural-language explanations (Huang et al., 2025b; Xu et al., 2025c; Chen et al., 2025c). More broadly, hierarchical multimodal reasoning workflows decompose complex interpretations into staged cognitive steps, providing useful precedent for structuring multimodal explanation pipelines (Huang et al., 2025a). In the separate explanation evaluation of Appendix H, language outputs describe fixed events and do not alter localization or detection decisions. Fluent descriptions do not themselves establish that predicted intervals or modality labels are correct, motivating separate evaluation of these outputs.

sections.content: We evaluate zero-shot and LoRA-tuned Qwen3-Omni explanation baselines conditioned on fixed events. We measure output validity, temporal agreement with reference intervals, operation/target identification, and abstention. These results show that event-conditioned explanation remains challenging: output validity and content correctness diverge, semantic identification remains low, and the tuned model abstains on most manipulated inputs.
